title: International shocks are absorbed through different public, private and cross-border buffers depending on development and fiscal capacity
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11345, Who Smooths the Shock? Government and Private Saving in International Risk Sharing
geography: 134 countries, covering advanced economies and emerging market and developing economies, 1990-2023

design.value: the paper decomposes how output shocks are smoothed through saving, cross-border income, transfers and other national-account channels

central_signal.value: savings are a central shock-smoothing mechanism, but the mix of public, private and cross-border channels differs sharply across country groups

observations.method: Panel analysis of 134 countries using an accounting-based decomposition of international risk sharing and income volatility.
observations.uncertainty: This is aggregate macroeconomic evidence; it does not identify which households receive protection, how quickly benefits arrive, or whether observed smoothing is welfare-improving.
observations.subgroup: Advanced economies, emerging markets and developing economies, governments, private savers, remittance-receiving households and countries with different fiscal and capital-account conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: More measured smoothing can reflect precautionary saving or compressed consumption rather than generous public protection; accounting shares do not by themselves establish policy causality.

observations.period: 1990-2023; advanced economies versus emerging market and developing economies

denominator.unit: broad country groups compared in the paper

advanced_economies.value: government saving absorbs about 14 percent of output shocks, exceeding the contribution of private saving
advanced_economies.unit: reported share of output shocks smoothed

emerging_and_developing.value: private saving smooths roughly 16 percent of output shocks compared with about 6 percent through government saving
emerging_and_developing.unit: reported share of output shocks smoothed

interpretation.value: the same global shock can reach households through different national buffers: public fiscal capacity in richer economies and private precautionary saving in EMDE

observations.method: Country-group comparison from the paper's national-account risk-sharing decomposition.
observations.uncertainty: The percentages are aggregate contributions, not the probability or magnitude of protection for an individual household, worker or firm.
observations.subgroup: Households and firms in advanced economies versus emerging and developing economies, with different access to public insurance and private liquidity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Private saving may indicate resilience, but it can also indicate that households must self-insure because public systems are thinner or less trusted.

denominator.unit: major country-group patterns identified in the paper

advanced_economies.value: primary investment income from abroad helps smooth income volatility mainly in advanced economies

emerging_and_developing.value: remittances and transfers help smooth income volatility mainly in emerging market and developing economies

social_meaning.value: migration, financial ownership and public or private transfers are part of the everyday infrastructure through which national shocks reach or are buffered from households

observations.method: Accounting decomposition of national income and cross-border risk-sharing components.
observations.uncertainty: The study does not estimate the distribution of remittance, transfer or investment-income gains within countries or their social costs.
observations.subgroup: Migrant-sending households, transfer recipients, asset owners, governments, financial intermediaries and countries integrated differently into global capital and labor flows.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cross-border channels can stabilize aggregate income while increasing dependence on migration, volatile capital markets or external policy decisions.

fiscal_space.value: countries with more fiscal space are better able to smooth output volatility through government saving

capital_openness.value: more open capital accounts shift the balance toward government-based stabilization and improve access to cross-border smoothing channels

program_implication.value: shock resilience depends not only on household behavior but also on whether governments have room to save, borrow, transfer and coordinate across borders

observations.method: Cross-country heterogeneity analysis relating the decomposition to fiscal space and capital-account openness.
observations.uncertainty: The paper reports relationships within an aggregate macro framework; it does not provide a clean causal estimate of a specific fiscal or financial reform.
observations.subgroup: Highly indebted governments, fiscally buffered governments, open and less-open economies, households exposed to public transfers and firms exposed to international finance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Openness may improve smoothing in some settings but can also transmit financial shocks faster; fiscal space can be politically contested and unevenly deployed.

related_sources.claim: World Bank reproducibility package describing the 134-country panel, 1990-2023 coverage, findings and computational verification.
Bibliographic record for World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11345 and its abstract.

boundary: This record adds a macro-to-household-buffer route linking international volatility to public saving, private precautionary saving, remittances, transfers, investment income, fiscal space and capital-account openness. It is aggregate accounting evidence, not respondent-level data, household causal evidence, a welfare evaluation or a forecast.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official World Bank working-paper PDF, World Bank reproducibility package and bibliographic abstract were reviewed for the country panel, country-group percentages, cross-border channels, fiscal-space relationship and methodological boundaries.
